author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Determine that the thing can and shall be done, and then we shall find the way.
work: Speech in the House of Representatives (20 June 1848)

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: The leading rule for the lawyer, as for the man of every other calling, is diligence. Leave nothing for to-morrow which can be done to-day.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Resolve to be honest at all events; and if in your own judgment you cannot be an honest lawyer, resolve to be honest without being a lawyer.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Upon the subject of education, not presuming to dictate any plan or system respecting it, I can only say that I view it as the most important subject which we as a people can be engaged in.
work: Address to the People of Sangamon County (9 March 1832)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Far and away the best prize that life offers is the chance to work hard at work worth doing.
work: Labor Day Address, New York State Agricultural Association, Syracuse (7 September 1903)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is not the critic who counts, not the man who points out how the strong man stumbled, or where the doer of deeds could have done better.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: In short, in life, as in a football game, the principle to follow is: Hit the line hard; don't foul and don't shirk, but hit the line hard!

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Be practical as well as generous in your ideals. Keep your eyes on the stars, but remember to keep your feet on the ground.
work: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I don't pity any man who does hard work worth doing. I admire him. I pity the creature who does not work, at whichever end of the social scale he may regard himself as being.
work: Remarks to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, Chattanooga (8 September 1902)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: We cannot avoid meeting great issues. All that we can determine for ourselves is whether we shall meet them well or ill.

author: George Washington
text: Be courteous to all, but intimate with few, and let those few be well tried before you give them your confidence; true friendship is a plant of slow growth.

author: George Washington
text: I hope I shall always possess firmness and virtue enough to maintain (what I consider the most enviable of all titles) the character of an honest man.

author: George Washington
text: It is better to offer no excuse than a bad one.

author: George Washington
text: Promote, then, as an object of primary importance, institutions for the general diffusion of knowledge.

author: George Washington
text: Discipline is the soul of an army. It makes small numbers formidable; procures success to the weak, and esteem to all.
work: Letter of Instructions to the Captains of the Virginia Regiments (29 July 1759)

author: Winston Churchill
text: Never give in — never, never, never, never, in nothing great or small, large or petty, never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others.
work: "Unlucky Alfonso", Collier's (27 June 1931); reprinted in Great Contemporaries (1937)

author: Winston Churchill
text: Personally, I am always ready to learn, although I do not always like being taught.
work: Speech in the House of Commons (4 November 1952)

author: Winston Churchill
text: To improve is to change, so to be perfect is to have changed often.
work: Speech in the House of Commons (23 June 1925)

author: Winston Churchill
text: Every day you may make progress. Every step may be fruitful. Yet there will stretch out before you an ever-lengthening, ever-ascending, ever-improving path.
work: "Painting as a Pastime", The Strand Magazine (1921–22)

author: Winston Churchill
text: Where my reason, imagination or interest were not engaged, I would not or I could not learn.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Resolution. Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Industry. Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Human felicity is produc'd not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: From a child I was fond of reading, and all the little money that came into my hands was ever laid out in books.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: For my own Part, when I am employed in serving others, I do not look upon myself as conferring Favours, but as paying Debts.

author: Peter Drucker
text: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things.

author: Peter Drucker
text: A superior who works on his own development sets an almost irresistible example.

author: Peter Drucker
text: A man should never be appointed into a managerial position if his vision focuses on people's weaknesses rather than on their strengths.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Morale in an organization does not mean that "people get along together"; the test is performance not conformance.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Effective executives do first things first and they do one thing at a time.
work: The Effective Executive, ch. 5 "First Things First" (1966)

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: What counts is not necessarily the size of the dog in the fight — it's the size of the fight in the dog.
work: Remarks at Republican National Committee Breakfast (31 January 1958)

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Humility must always be the portion of any man who receives acclaim earned in blood of his followers and sacrifices of his friends.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The essence of leadership is to get others to do something because they think you want it done and because they know it is worth while doing.
work: Remarks at the Republican Campaign Picnic, Gettysburg Farm (12 September 1956)

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Leadership consists of nothing but taking responsibility for everything that goes wrong and giving your subordinates credit for everything that goes well.
work: Interview in Edgar F. Puryear Jr., Nineteen Stars (1971)

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.
work: Remarks at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference (14 November 1957)

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I learned the lesson that great men cultivate love, and that only little men cherish a spirit of hatred.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: Nothing ever comes to me, that is worth having, except as the result of hard work.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: In meeting men, in many places, I have found that the happiest people are those who do the most for others; the most miserable are those who do the least.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: If there is no struggle, there is no progress. Those who profess to favor freedom, and yet depreciate agitation, are men who want crops without plowing up the ground.
work: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York (August 1857)

author: Frederick Douglass
text: I would unite with anybody to do right; and with nobody to do wrong.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 10 (1845)

author: Frederick Douglass
text: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 6 (1845)

author: Frederick Douglass
text: My theory of self-made men is, then, simply this: that they are men of work.
work: Self-Made Men, address at Carlisle Indian Industrial School (c. 1893)
